body_html:
How to think about it

A cell changes chemical energy into electrical energy. Current (A) is measured with an ammeter in series; potential difference (V) with a voltmeter in parallel. Resistance (Ω) opposes current: a longer or thinner wire has more resistance.

In series, the current is the same everywhere and the potential differences add up. In parallel, the potential difference across each branch is the same and the currents add up. Fuses and circuit breakers cut the current if it is too high. Electricity is sold in kilowatt-hours: energy = power × time, cost = kWh × price per kWh.

Example

A 2 kW heater runs for 3 h. How much energy does it use?

kWh = kW × h

Answer: 6 kWh

Example

What does a fuse do?

It melts.

Answer: breaks the circuit if the current is too high

Common mistakes

  • Putting the voltmeter in series.
  • Thinking a thinner wire has less resistance.
  • Mixing up watts and kilowatt-hours.

faq.q: Why is an electric kettle expensive to use for a long time?
faq.a: It has a high power rating, so it uses many kWh.

faq.q: Why does a geyser use so much electricity?
faq.a: Heating water needs a lot of energy; a solar geyser or timer saves money.

items.q: Two lamps are in series with a 6 V battery. The voltmeter across one lamp reads 3 V. What does it read across the other lamp?
items.e: In series the potential difference is shared: 6 − 3.

items.q: A lamp is in a circuit with a cell. The resistance of the variable resistor is decreased. What happens?
c: The total resistance increases, so the current decreases and both lamps are dimmer.
Each branch has the full voltage, so each lamp stays as bright and the total current increases.
The current is used up by the lamp.
The current increases and the lamp becomes brighter.
